title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
description: Given an array `nums` of positive integers, decide whether it can be split into two groups with **equal sums**. Every element must go to exactly one group.

examples.explanation: The total is 11, which is odd, so no equal split exists.

hints: If the total is odd the answer is immediately false. Otherwise you need a subset summing to total / 2.
This is 0/1 knapsack feasibility: reachable[s] = can some subset sum to s. Process each number once and update sums from high to low so an element is not reused.
In Python a single integer can be the whole bitset: bits |= bits << x. Check bit total//2 at the end.
approach:
**Reduce to subset-sum: does any subset sum to exactly half the total?** If the total is odd, no. Otherwise this is 0/1 knapsack feasibility. Let `reach[s]` be true when some subset of the elements processed so far sums to `s`. Adding element `x` makes `reach[s] |= reach[s - x]`; iterate `s` downward so that the same element is not counted twice.

Representing `reach` as a Python integer bitset turns the whole inner loop into `bits |= bits << x`, which is both the fastest and the shortest version; mention the boolean-array form (`for s in range(target, x-1, -1)`) so the interviewer sees you know what the shift is doing.

**Why it works:** after processing a prefix of `nums`, the set bits are exactly the achievable subset sums of that prefix, by induction: a sum of the longer prefix either omits `x` (already set) or includes it (set at `s - x` before this step).

**Common mistakes:** iterating sums upward with a 1-D array (lets an element be reused, turning it into unbounded knapsack), forgetting the odd-total shortcut, and recursing over all 2^n subsets.

**Interview follow-ups:** Reconstruct one of the two groups? (Keep a 2-D table `reach[i][s]` or a `parent` bitset per step, then walk back; O(n * target) space.) Partition into k equal groups? (Bitmask DP over subsets, or backtracking with pruning.) Minimise the difference between the two group sums? (Largest reachable s <= total // 2.) Can you bound the running time by the value range instead of n * target? (Yes: target <= 10^4 here, so the bitset has at most 10^4 bits.)

complexity.time: O(n * total / w) with word size w (O(n * total) in the array form)
